hints: Look carefully at the starting tube. The heavy $^{15}$N DNA forms a band at M, right at the bottom, so K at the top must be light DNA and L in the middle must be in between.
Remember DNA replicates semi-conservatively, so think about what each new double helix contains after one round of copying a heavy helix using only light $^{14}$N nucleotides.
walkthrough:
**Work out what K, L and M mean**

This is the famous Meselson and Stahl experiment. Heavier DNA sinks lower in the tube.

So M at the bottom = heavy-heavy ($^{15}$N-$^{15}$N), K at the top = light-light ($^{14}$N-$^{14}$N), and L in the middle = hybrid ($^{15}$N-$^{14}$N).

**Predict after dividing once in light nitrogen**

You start with all heavy DNA. Replication is semi-conservative, so each helix unwinds and each old heavy strand is used as a template to build a new light strand.

Result: every DNA molecule is one old heavy strand plus one new light strand. That is all hybrid DNA, so you see one band, all at L.

**Predict after dividing twice in light nitrogen**

Now those hybrid molecules replicate again in $^{14}$N. The heavy strand makes another hybrid, but the light strand makes a fully light molecule.

Result: half the DNA is hybrid (at L) and half is light (at K). That matches all at L, then half at K and half at L.

options.A: Two bands after one division would mean conservative replication, not semi-conservative. In reality all molecules are identical hybrids after one division.
options.B: You never get light (K) and heavy (M) together with no hybrid after one division. Semi-conservative replication gives only hybrid molecules at this stage.
options.C: Correct. After one division all DNA is $^{15}$N-$^{14}$N hybrid at L, and after two divisions it is half hybrid at L and half light $^{14}$N-$^{14}$N at K.
options.D: All at M after one division would mean no new light nucleotides were used. In fact every new strand is made with light $^{14}$N, so mass must decrease.
